blocks.text: He passes also the walls of ancient Carthaea on Ceos, where the father Alcidamas was to marvel that a gentle dove could be born from the body of his daughter.
7. In the same author (Metam. book 13, Fable 4), the Oenotropae, daughters of Anius, as their father Anius tells Anchises,
— — — took on wings, and were turned into the snow-white birds of your consort, doves.

That is, into the birds of Venus, who had been the consort of Anchises. These stories, however fabulous, nevertheless serve our purpose. For from them you may at least gather that, in the opinion of those who invented these fables, there had always been doves in Greece. 8. What of the fact that Homer calls Boeotian Thisbe and Laconian Messene πολυτρήρωνας [polytērōnas], from their abundance of doves, Iliad 2? And Pliny, book 5, chapter 31, lists near Smyrna seven islands called Peristerides, that is, Columbariae [Dove Islands]. It is therefore very likely that after the Flood doves first made their way into Greece and the neighbouring places, and from there were gradually dispersed over the rest of the world.

You will say that these things are adduced in vain, since in those most ancient times after the Flood Syria too was πολυτρήρονα [polytērona], as is proved both from sacred and from profane histories. For in the sacred histories Abraham, than whom the Greeks have nothing more ancient, is commanded to offer to God a turtledove and a dove, Gen. XV, 9. And throughout the Law of Moses sacrifices of turtledoves and young doves are prescribed [II, 528]. For examples see Levit. I, 14. and V, 7. 11. and XII, 6. and XIV, 22. and XXV, 14. 29. and Num. VI, 10. In the profane histories too, Semiramis, believed to be a contemporary of Abraham, is said to have been exposed in desert and rocky places near Ascalon, ἐν οἷς πολλοῦ πλήθους περιστερῶν ἐννοσσεύειν εἰωθότος, παραδόξως τροφῆς καὶ σωτηρίας τυχεῖν τὸ βρέφος [en hois pollou plēthous peristerōn ennosseuein eiōthotos, paradoxōs trophēs kai sōtērias tychein to brephos], where, since a great multitude of doves was accustomed to nest, the infant was wondrously fed and preserved. Indeed, the name of Semiramis is derived from the same source, as being κατὰ τὴν τῶν Σύρων διάλεκτον παρωνομασμένον ἀπὸ τῶν περιστερῶν [kata tēn tōn Syrōn dialekton parōnomasmenon apo tōn peristerōn], taken from doves in the language of the Syrians. So Diodorus, from Ctesias, in book 2. And R. Azarias, in Meor Enajim, chapter 21, derives it from the word זמיר zemir, which denotes the song of birds, and specifically of the turtledove, Cant. II, 12. His words are as follows: נקראת סמיראמיס אשר לפי דבריו בלשון הארמי יורה על צפצוף העוף ולדעתי הוא מלשון עת הזמיר הגיע בחלוף הזין בסמך וכן בארמי פק דנטין זמרא דמנא זמרא דפומא ולזה אות דגלה היה יונה She is called Semiramis, which, according to his words, (that is, those of Diodorus, whom he had cited) signifies in the Syrian language the song of birds. This seems to be taken from the word זמיר zemir, as it is said in Cant. II, 12. [col. 5] "The time of zemir, that is, of song, has come, and the voice of the turtledove is heard in our land." For also in Syriac, in the Talmudic tractate Gittin, chapter 1, זמרא דמנא zemara demana is instrumental music, and זמרא דפומא zemara dephuma vocal music. And therefore Semiramis had a dove as the emblem of her banner. Indeed, he contends in what follows that not only Semiramis but all the kings of Assyria had a dove as the symbol of their banners. And that this is why, for the wrath and sword of the Assyrians, Jeremiah had said חרון היונה, the wrath of the dove, Ierem. XXV, 38. and חרב היונה, the sword of the dove, Ierem. XLVI, 16, and L, 16. This he confirms from the version of Jerome and from the Commentaries of Thomas Aquinas on Jeremiah. To the same he also refers the fact that Jerusalem in Sophon. III, 1. is called היונה, the dove, as if the Prophet were reproaching her שהיא במעשיו דומה לבבל אשר אות דגלה יונה, that in her deeds she is like Babylon, which had a dove on its banner as its military emblem. And following him, R. David Ganz, in book 2 of his Chronology, at the year 1958: The emblem of the banner of Semiramis was the figure of a dove. This banner emblem all the kings of Assyria imitated. Hence Jeremiah, chapter XXV, verse 28: "Because of the wrath of the dove"; and chapter XLVI, verse 6: "Before the sword of the dove". To this the ancients add that Semiramis was changed into a dove. Diodorus, in the place cited above: Ἔνιοι δὲ μυθολογοῦντές φασιν αὐτὴν γενέσθαι περιστερὰν, καὶ πολλῶν ὀρνέων εἰς τὴν οἰκίαν καταπετασθέντων, μετ᾽ ἐκείνων ἐκπετασθῆναι· [Enioi de mythologountes phasin autēn genesthai peristeran, kai pollōn orneōn eis tēn oikian katapetasthentōn, met᾽ ekeinōn ekpetasthēnai] But others tell the fable that she became a dove, and that when many birds had flown into the house, she flew away with them.
